extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets and prose writers; literary students and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and judging prose, poetry, drama, and other arts—focusing on diction, unity, imitation vs. copy, execution, and the role of feeling/thought. Drawn from 19th‑century literary criticism and advice to creative writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tightly integrated word-collocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The collocation of words in the great masters (Shakspeare, Milton) is so artificial and integral that you cannot remove a word without harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat finished passages as mosaic work: 'The amotion or transposition will alter the thought, or the feeling, or at least the tone. They are as pieces of mosaic work, from which you cannot strike the smallest block without making a hole in the picture.' Edit with extreme care; individual words may be essential to tone and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good prose = proper words in proper places
rubrics_metrics.description: Good prose uses 'proper words in their proper places'; words should express the intended meaning and no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prose diction should be unobtrusive so the reader understands without noticing the medium. If words draw attention to themselves in prose, it is generally a fault. Aim for clarity and fitness of diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good verse = the most proper words in place (beauty + unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In verse the words (the media) must be beautiful and attract notice, but not so much as to destroy the unity of the whole poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry requires elevated diction but must still preserve a unity of impression. Excessive pointiness or profusion of striking parts can prevent the overall unity; balance ornament with cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of impression (poetry and drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great thing in poetry (and tragic drama) is to effect a unity of impression upon the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements (chorus, comic scenes, fools) must contribute to the overall effect rather than disrupt it. Example: Shakespeare integrates comic elements (the Fool in Lear) to enhance tragic unity; Beaumont & Fletcher sometimes fail, producing hybrids lacking unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate modulation of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the degree of 'media' prominence to genre: oratory may border on verse (more studied media), narrative verse should be simpler, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust diction and rhetorical display to the subgenre—some prose (oratory) may legitimately be more ornate; some verse may be more narrative and simpler. Know the norms and expectations of the sub-form you are writing in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stylistic extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the faults of extremes—e.g., Cavalier slang on one hand and Johnsonian magniloquence on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful lesson in style is to examine extremes and understand how each is faulty; aim for balance between colloquiality and bombast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation = balance of likeness and difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is a mesothesis of likeness and difference; the difference is as essential as the likeness—without it imitation becomes mere copy or facsimile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When imitating masters, keep enough distinctness so your work is not a facsimile. Imitation should verge toward likeness in some arts (painting) and toward difference in others (sculpture)—but difference remains crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality over mere realism/likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely making a figure 'stand out of the canvass' or producing exact likeness (as with wax figures) is inferior to an imitation that means something for the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portraiture and literary depiction, realism alone (perfect likeness) gives limited pleasure; aim to represent the ideal or the thought behind the form—seek significance beyond surface accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must possess thought or feeling (not only sensual appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should show thought or feeling; mere addresses to the sensual ear (or eye) are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's taste dismissed works that catered only to sensual gratification (e.g., Rossini) and praised those with intellectual or emotional depth (Beethoven, Mozart). Writers should aim for works that engage mind or heart, not only surface pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution matters more in some styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Some styles (e.g., Gothic architecture as 'infinity made imaginable') depend much more on execution for their effect than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain aesthetic modes demand exceptional technical execution to realize their sublime aims; strive for high craftsmanship where the style requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of comic and tragic elements must serve the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic scenes intermixed in tragedy are a fault unless they produce a unity of the tragic on the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comic relief only when it enhances the overall tragic effect (as Shakespeare does); careless intermixture can create hybrid plays lacking coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization via others' testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's skill can create sympathy for a character indirectly—by having other characters praise and commend them—thereby guiding readers to like them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character development may rely on social context and the reactions of other characters; this can be a deliberate technique to engender audience sympathy when direct depiction is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness of sensation—present familiar objects anew
rubrics_metrics.description: A prime merit of genius is to represent familiar objects so as to awaken in others a kindred freshness of sensation (carrying child's wonder into adult powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to renew the reader's perception of commonplace things; retaining a child's sense of wonder within mature craft distinguishes genius from mere talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic productivity is aided by encouragement and sympathetic audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets require sympathy and expressed hope (applause) as nourishment; without it the sense of power dwindles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the social and psychological conditions that sustain creative work—encouragement and reception can materially affect a poet's ability to produce and sustain effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the limits of theory and the role of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of theory (analogy for creative method) is to collect and help view known facts; it assists investigation but cannot invent truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative practice, theories or methods should organize and illuminate observed material but not replace direct engagement with particulars; remain open to revising theory when new facts (experiences, readings) emerge.
